title: Great Teaching Can’t Compensate for a Broken System
summary:
Great Teaching Can’t Compensate for a Broken System

I used to believe that knowledgeable and skilled teachers would be the solution to low literacy rates. In training sessions for teachers, I often displayed a quote from Maya Angelou:

Do the best you can until you know better. Then when you know better, do better.

I aimed to give teachers the professional development that I wished I had received. I had no idea how unfair it is to assume that teachers can get better results while working within a system that doesn’t support us.

Knowing better isn’t enough

An example:

Despite learning about the problems with predictable books, primary grade teachers in my Community of Practice were keeping leveled books in their classrooms. At first, I assumed that they needed more training about how to teach decoding and why the F&P leveling system was problematic.

But soon I realized the problem wasn’t the teachers — not their knowledge and not their skill.

Teachers were keeping predictable books in their classrooms because:

  • Removing leveled libraries felt wasteful and their schools had limited resources.
  • They imagined they might have to bring the materials back if “the pendulum” of reading instruction swung the other way.
  • They didn’t have replacement books for students to enjoy during their school’s “drop everything and read” time.
  • They worried they’d be evaluated poorly by district leaders if bins with leveled books weren’t visible during “walk-throughs.”

So leveled libraries had to stay put in the classrooms despite teachers “knowing better.” I told myself that as long as they weren’t being used for instruction, it was no big deal.

But soon, I discovered that many teachers were still teaching with predictable books. I came to see that the system around us implicitly required Guided Reading:

  • Teachers were expected to regularly assess students’ reading levels using the Fountas & Pinnell Benchmark Assessment System
  • They knew that students who couldn’t “read” predictable books would fail the assessment
  • They had to add students’ reading levels to their school’s data tracker every two weeks
  • District report cards required that they include each child’s reading level using the F&P system
  • Parents asked teachers, “What’s my child’s reading level?”

Pressures to continue Guided Reading could not be overridden by my training or coaching of teachers. The system that determined what school schedules prioritized, how teachers were evaluated, and the data that was collected and displayed out-powered the teachers’ knowledge and skill.

There’s a science behind this conundrum

Implementation Science describes drivers(opens in a new window), the forces that shape what people actually do day-to-day. The three categories of drivers are:

Competency drivers: how practitioners are selected, trained, and coached

Organization drivers: the data systems, policies, and leadership structures that support the work

Leadership driver: who is steering and how

Strength in one driver can partially offset weakness in another. A highly skilled, well-coached teacher can work within a weak system for a while, but eventually we realize that our job is more difficult than it ought to be and the results we’re getting aren’t as good as they should be. We burn out and many of us leave the profession.

Implementation drivers must reinforce each other 

When one driver is missing or misaligned, it creates drag on the others. Poorly developed district systems create problems for teachers and school site leaders, just as poorly run schools and classrooms can drag down the quality of district initiatives.

Bottom up? Top down? Actually, neither

I used to think that a grassroots effort, led by knowledgeable and skilled classroom teachers, was the way to improve reading instruction at scale. I believed this because top-down initiatives such as Reading First and No Child Left Behind had failed to shift teachers’ daily instruction. But I’ve learned from Implementation Science that I was wrong. According to the science, sequentially improving the drivers (building teacher competence followed by district leadership or vice versa) doesn’t work. They must be improved simultaneously to get results. 

Even the highest-quality training of teachers can’t defend against a dysfunctional system. And the best-laid policy won’t result in academic gains if teachers aren’t supported in their classrooms.

Getting it right

So what would happen if highly-skilled teachers worked in a functional system that had good leadership? How might education be transformed? We would eliminate the barriers that impede our ability to teach all children to read.

  • We’d set clear expectations for what teachers should know and be able to do, and provide compensation that reflects the skills required. 
  • Teacher preparation programs would move away from theory-heavy coursework toward clinical training, demonstrating what good instruction looks like, letting us practice, and giving feedback so we can improve.
  • Teacher contracts would be more standardized, ensuring adequate time and compensation for the planning, coaching, and professional development we need to build new skills and transfer them to classroom instruction.
  • We’d end the system’s churn through teachers and administrators. Our persistent “teacher shortage” is not a shortage of credentialed people — it’s a shortage of people willing to teach in poor conditions for low pay.
  • School schedules would change to accommodate dedicated time, as needed, for in-classroom coaching for teachers and intervention for students.
  • Quality-control measures would be put in place so that only research-based, implementable programs are permitted in schools.
  • Leadership training programs would develop administrators who understand implementation science and evidence-based instruction — and who can create the conditions teachers and students need to succeed.

If we expect teachers to have training and skills equivalent to engineers, then we need to pay them like engineers.Reid Lyon

Each of these changes will require coordination across every level of the system and none of them will happen on their own, but Implementation Science can guide the improvement process.

We can’t wait

Other professions waited for a visible crisis to force change — a shipwreck, a market crash. (For more on this, I recommend Why Education Experts Resist Effective Practices (And What It Would Take To Make Education More Like Medicine(opens in a new window).) Education’s crisis has been here for decades, evident in low student achievement and high teacher turnover. 

We don’t need to wait for a dramatic catalyst to allow scientific evidence to guide education. We can choose to learn from the science of reading and the science of implementation, and apply both — not just to how we teach reading, but to how we build the systems in which teaching happens.

title: What We Talk About When We Talk About the Love of Reading: Part 2
summary:
What We Talk About When We Talk About the Love of Reading: Part 2

In my last blog, What We Talk About When We Talk About the Love of Reading: Part 1, I replied to a teacher’s question about teaching a love of reading. She noted the many recent reports of declines in pleasure reading (e.g., Horowitch, 2026).

I pointed out that this decline is not just a recent trend, but one that stretches back more than 80 years (Bone, Bu, Sonke, & Fancourt, 2006). I also noted that not only are Americans reading less, but the same is true in the United Kingdom and Australia (Cremin & Scholes, 2024).

Of three possible reasons for the downturn, my analysis suggested that we can’t blame it on low reading ability or lack of opportunity.

The idea of “pleasure reading” is somewhat amorphous. That’s why it often gets mixed up with fiction reading. Some people seemingly can’t imagine anyone reading history, biography, cookbooks, or technical manuals for enjoyment, though many of us do just that. One wonders if survey respondents are also confused by this — claiming they don’t read for pleasure because they don’t read fiction

That same kind of confusion was apparent in older surveys when it came to digital reading. It wasn’t clear what counted as reading. Recent surveys make a clearer distinction between traditional books and e-books (Montgomery, 2025), so both now get counted. But I’d bet that the reading of social media still is not, though it is reading (St. Aubin & Liedke, 2025).

Nevertheless, it seems likely that there has been a real downward shift in our reading habits.

There are two possible reasons for this — either we’re no longer pursuing the goals that we once read for, or the availability of other media sources now make it possible to accomplish those goals as well or better than before without reading.

The easy availability of screens suggests it’s the latter. Someone killing time perusing a newspaper or magazine over their morning coffee or while waiting for the dentist, may now view videoclips on their phones instead. Such viewing fills the time every bit as well as reading once did.

Why should we care whether people read? Not “why is it important for people to know how to read?” or “why does it matter that they engage in the reading needed for their work or to participate in our communities as citizens?” The answers to those questions are obvious. But does it matter that my neighbor reads, or reads books, or reads fiction?

There are lots of claims about why reading matters: it fosters empathy and perspective taking; improves critical thinking; builds vocabulary, language, and communication skills; allows for anticipation and rehearsal of experiences; strengthens memory and cognition; builds knowledge; reduces stress and improves sleep; builds problem solving skills; provides a sense of support and belonging (Barker, 2024).

That’s an impressive list. Some of those claims are even supported by evidence. For instance, it’s clear that reading enhances language by helping readers to increase their vocabularies (Wasik, Hindman, & Snell, 2016). That’s also true for other media such as TV viewing, but text language tends to be much more challenging than the language presented by other sources, so it is probably the best way to enhance language (Kucker, Barr, & Perry, 2026).  

We can learn things from our reading as well, so the notion that it increases knowledge is a no-brainer. Many claims about the benefits of reading focus on its ability to transport readers to different places and different times. That makes sense but just means that there are certain kinds of knowledge that reading may increase. It is reasonable to point out that one can build knowledge — including those specific types — through other media, though texts can be more detailed and extensive than what we usually experience through those other sources.

There are studies showing reading to be an effective and efficient tension reliever (Lewis, 2009). Maybe that reading in the dentist office isn’t just for killing time. But it’s fair to point out that listening to music can have a similar effect, though apparently it takes music longer to work its magic.

Certainly, reading about things that haven’t happened or haven’t happened to us allows us to imagine how we might respond in the future. But that seems equally true of films and other media.

The idea that reading fosters empathy and perspective taking has been a popular claim. One widely noted study found that this only happened with the reading of literary fiction but not with popular fiction or non-fiction (Kidd & Castano, 2013). In other words, if you read Jane Austin you’ll become a better person, but that won’t happen if you read Danielle Steele. At least that’s what’s purported. Examining all the research on this issue suggests caution (Denham, 2024), and these same benefits have been accomplished by watching video narratives (Rohm, Hopp, & Smit, 2022).

The claims about reading’s purported positive impacts on critical thinking, memory, and cognition are supported only by correlational evidence. You can’t tell if reading fosters those abilities or if those who are gifted in those areas are more likely to be readers. It is true that studies have found that more areas of the brain “light up” or are activated during reading than while watching television (Rauschecker, Nedelec, Pan, Olaru, Nillo, Palmer, Pecheva, Dale, Jernigan, & Sugrue, 2025).

The unsubstantiated idea that reading accords a sense of belonging seems to contradict actual data — remember the study discussed in my previous blog — teens who read more were less happy than those who read less, probably because of the isolation from social participation that it often requires (Csikszentmihalyi & Hunter, 2003).

Rarely do these hagiographies of reading champion that idea of social isolation as a plus. Years ago, I did workshops on motivating reading. My audiences were mostly elementary teachers — so they tended to be predominately women. I would ask why they read, and the number one response was the separation that it provided. These women taught all day, and then came home and prepared dinner, dealt with children and husbands and they saw reading as a much-needed escape from meeting the needs of everyone else. Reading gave them a chance to recharge and heal. They often read what may be characterized as junk and they were embarrassed about this, but they weren’t looking to sharpen their critical thinking or to gain deep knowledge about anything. They just wanted to get away, to claw out a bit of me-time. I suspect a good deal of television viewing and net surfing fills that role, too.

One more benefit that might not get sufficient attention is the aesthetic pleasure that certain texts can provide. Anyone who has luxuriated in the language of Shakespeare or Faulkner knows of what I speak. It’s possible to admire the beauty of language by listening to the radio or watching a film, but those media make it clumsy to dwell on the beauty or to review the gorgeous parts.  

What sense do I make of all that?

I think reading is valuable because it can contribute to our lives in so many ways. But newer technologies and media sources have developed that can address the same needs or help us solve the same problems. Sometimes the new alternatives may do a better job, in other cases they pale by comparison — but, at least for some people, those alternatives are acceptable. Given that, we should expect people to read less or to read different kinds of texts than in the past, and that is not necessarily a problem.

Where it becomes one is with youngsters. As noted, reading can improve language — and this includes increasing one’s reading and writing proficiency. I might not be worried about my neighbors who’d rather watch the movie than read the book, but I am concerned about their children who may be blowing reading off, too. If those kids are going to reach the levels of reading that we hope for them, they will need to practice more.  

In the previous blog post, I noted the many efforts teachers have made to encourage reading, such as “drop everything and read” times during school days. Such efforts haven’t borne much fruit. Those periods just swap one kind of reading for another. We’re making reading part of our lives, not part of the kids’ lives. Ultimately, it’s the youngster who will have to decide to turn off Roblox and pick up a book or magazine.

What can we do?

First, we should stop avoiding literacy during the school day — and this is not just a K-12 complaint. Schools devote a lot of time to the teaching of reading, writing, and spelling. But then we often avoid reading during math, social studies, science, and the arts. Teachers work around the books in so many ways — telling students what they say, reading them to the kids, and just skipping them altogether.

Recent reports out of the universities is that college students won’t do the reading, so professors have cut back on reading requirements (Baier, Hendricks, Gorden, Hendricks, & Cochran, 2011). What they should be doing is making sure the reading assignments contribute to learning and then hold students accountable for this — by having discussions of the material in class, perhaps led by students, and holding them accountable for the text-based information through quizzes and tests.

Second, we need to promote reading outside of school, encouraging parents to get their kids reading. Recent surveys show that the amount of parent reading to young children hasn’t declined over the past couple of decades — it’s the one kind of reading that has not lessened. That sounds like something to celebrate, but the same surveys reveal that few parents have ever read to their children (Bone, Bu, Sonke, & Fancourt, 2006). Pediatrician-based programs like Reach Out and Read have shown that we can make headway with parents, and schools should find ways to encourage this too. Schools often know which families have kids who haven’t yet started school and can provide encouragement, books, and other supports (like parent workshops). Those actions can make a big difference. Local libraries often provide terrific programming aimed at getting young children involved with books, but too often those efforts are not coordinated with the schools.

Many parents are not aware of the importance of their children’s reading practice, so if their kids resist they back down. Providing information to the community about the value of reading can stiffen the backbones of parents. This kind of information and encouragement may be even more needed with the older students. Lots of moms and dads will focus on their kids’ reading when they are first learning to read, but they tend to back off pretty quickly after that. Big mistake. Encouragement from the schools can keep them engaged.

Third, recently there has been a major push in literacy education to make sure that the texts used for teaching reading include content that we hope the kids will master; building knowledge. This has led to reading programs that include units framed around topics based on social studies and science standards. Nothing wrong with that, though I’m concerned that, at least in some cases, the role that literature can play in fostering knowledge (both literary and psychosocial) is being elbowed out of the picture.

However, I also think that it would be useful for students to spend some time building knowledge about literacy and its uses. Once upon a time, when I was a reading consultant in a school district, we had a weekly period in which students studied literacy. They engaged in homework activities in which they tried to identify all the uses of reading and writing that they could find and bring in the evidence. This led to kids collecting notes, magazines, books, newspapers, baseball cards, menus, parking tickets, mail, recipes, cereal boxes, pictures of road signs, and so on. In class, these items would be discussed, and their uses would be evaluated in terms of their who, what, where, why, and how. Perhaps we should have engaged them in planning and conducting interviews with people about what and why they read.

Imagine a classroom in which the kids are studying literacy. The teacher shares that research indicating that the reading of certain kinds of literature increases empathy and perspective taking, explaining how that is supposed to work (e.g., stories allow us to get inside the heads of characters, for instance). Then they read R. J. Palacio’s Wonder, to engage in that kind of compassion centered literacy to experience it and to ponder how it may generalize to their lives outside of books, and why that would matter.

These same kids, after discussions about the importance and value of reading, may be asked to document their own reading for some length of time. This could lead to discussions about the sacrifices reading sometimes requires, considering why it might be worth it anyway.

When it comes to kids, I think one of the most important ideas about literacy that should be explored is its social role. Does reading isolate you or connect you to others? Some experts encourage kids to read at home but then to bring what they have learned or experienced from it to school to share with their peers. Other experts encourage book clubs and reading groups to get kids to connect to others through their reading. The tension between reading to escape to other places and other times and reading to relate to others is a worthwhile literacy topic for kids to study and debate.

Reading is not done for reading’s sake. Most reading is done to accomplish other purposes or goals. I don’t think we do enough to make certain that kids understand all the ways that they could use reading. If we want people to read more, we need to make sure they recognize its possibilities and value. Technology may be replacing or reducing some kinds of reading, allowing people to accomplish certain goals that in the past would have depended on reading. But there are good reasons to believe that technology cannot take the place of some kinds of reading, or that it is an imperfect replacement in others.

We need to make sure that our kids know not just that we want them to read, but why we think this is so important — and then we must make those uses of reading accessible.

title: Making Space for Curiosity
summary:
Making Space for Curiosity

What did curiosity spark with your young readers this summer? In our house, it was robots. Specifically, could a robot with a camera be programmed to follow the cat around and record his antics? Why yes, it could — and, surprisingly, the cat was amused.

Watching my kids relish their uncertainty as they tested and retested the robot was a highlight of the summer. Though it might seem more challenging to make space for curiosity without the freer days of summer, the start of a new school year is an important time to think about how we can continue to spark and grow kids’ curiosity. Jane Kurtz(opens in a new window)’s guest post below is a wonderful example of where curiosity can lead when we follow our questions and passions — and a great model for both adults and young readers!

Thanks to her own curiosity, award-winning author Jane Kurtz has published more than 40 books — fiction and nonfiction, picture books and novels. In addition to being a curious writer, Jane is also an ambassador for literacy — especially in her childhood home of Ethiopia. She is one of the founders of Ethiopia Reads(opens in a new window), which has developed more than 80 libraries for children in Ethiopia, and also of Ready Set Go Books(opens in a new window), a program of Open Hearts Big Dreams(opens in a new window), that produces and distributes local language early readers to Ethiopian children.

Jane’s story and the stories she writes are excellent reminders of what can happen when we embrace the wonders of the world and keep asking questions about how things work and why.

What Is It about Dinosaurs? by Jane Kurtz

I’m eight years old. The canvas tent smells faintly like campfire smoke as my sisters and I help Daddy put it up. Wind is brushing against the cottonwood leaves. 

I can’t stop thinking about what we saw — huge bones in a wall, as if a dragon had landed and rocks had gently folded around it.

I was a fairy tale kid. I knew my stuffed animals would never actually talk and those ferns with curled tips wouldn’t ever shake off their enchantment, but dragons had to be somewhere.

And here they were. Real.

I walked out of the gift shop with smooth Brontosaurus, thunder lizard, in my pocket. Recently, I tried to capture that scene in my almost true story in verse, Oh Give Me A Home(opens in a new window). It has always stayed with me.

Much later, I had kids.

For my older son, it was the stomping and roaring. Especially T. rex.

For my younger son, it was the delight of memorizing the names.

We read books. We went camping and listened to park rangers explain about the meteor hurtling toward Earth. Poof. No more dinosaurs.

When one of my editors asked if I had ideas for a ready-to-read book about a real person, I thought about T. rex again. Who uncovered that amazing head? Those tiny arms? Ah-hah! It was Barnum Brown, the man they said could smell dinosaur bones. I went to see the skeleton he dug up in Montana, now at the American Museum of Natural History.

My book, Mr. Bones(opens in a new window), let me ask kids what they were curious about when it came to dinosaurs. I got to talk about good questions and how research is like a treasure hunt. I’d felt left out of science classes as a kid—too busy reading my fairy tales and pretending I was a horse. I thought science was about memorizing names like pistil and stamen and writing labels on worksheets.

Somehow dinosaurs had still gotten to me.

As an adult, I slowly fell in love with true stories told in interesting ways. Eventually, I published my first picture book that was labeled nonfiction: What Do They Do with All That Poo?(opens in a new window)

I told the editor of my poo book that I was reading a book for grown-ups about whatever happened to Brontosaurus. Did she know scientists were now studying dinosaur poo? I said I wanted to write next about dinosaur poo.

She said, “I want to know what happened to Brontosaurus.” Many drafts later, she published The Bone Wars: The True Story of an Epic Battle to Find Dinosaur Fossils(opens in a new window). Now I could share with kids an understanding of science as a drive to solve puzzles and explore mysteries. We could discuss how O.C. Marsh and Edward Cope ruined their lives, each fiercely wanting to name ALL THE DINOSAURS.

Not one to give up easily, I also flew to Colorado and interviewed Dr. Karen Chin about studying coprolites, fossilized poo. I asked if I could write a picture book biography with and about her. At first, she felt shy about the idea. But then she said she wanted kids to have models of scientists who look like her. So, we worked together on The Clues Are in the Poo: The Story of Dinosaur Scientist Karen Chin(opens in a new window). Now I had conversations with kids about what the world was like around dinosaurs and also about how people become scientists.

Honestly, I’m amazed that I’ve gotten to be this old without really understanding the ancient earth. Dinosaur bones fascinated me long ago. But Dr. Chin gave me context.

Once, she told me that some people mistakenly think O.C. Marsh came up with the name coprolite as a dig at his rival, Edward Cope. I started to read about the man who did invent that word. William Buckland also named the first dinosaur before the word dinosaur was invented. As I was reading about his boisterous, outrageous, science-y household full of children and animals, I got intrigued by his wife, Mary Morland, her fascination with fossils and drawing and experiments. Mary Morland in the Time of Dinosaur Discovery(opens in a new window) turned into a way to talk about history: the days when women didn’t go to school, the days when jumbles of old bones were being puzzled together and figured out.

What is it about dinosaurs? I know they’re my door into science. I’ll never stop wanting to learn about them and share the true stories of what I find out.

title: What We Talk About When We Talk About the Love of Reading: Part 1
summary:
What We Talk About When We Talk About the Love of Reading: Part 1

Teacher question

I’m an avid reader of your blog. I know that your focus is on teaching reading, but what about fostering a love of reading? Recently, the news has reported that no one is reading anymore. Shouldn’t we do something about that?

Shanahan’s response

You’re right about the recent news. The headlines have been incessant:

  • A Third of Americans Say They’re Reading Fewer Books (CBS News)
  • Gen Z is Reading Less. What That Means in the Age of Ready Answers. (Forbes)
  • Reading for Pleasure is Sharply Down Among Schoolkids, Report Shows. (NBC News)
  • Fewer People Are Reading for Fun, Study Finds (New York Times) 
  • Reading for Pleasure in Free Fall: New Study Finds 40% Drop Over Two Decades (University of Florida News)
  • Is the decline in reading books making us dumber? (The Economist)
  • Reading for pleasure builds empathy in children, but fewer kids are picking up books just for the fun of it (The Conversation)

If you dig down into those accounts you’ll find statistics that are every bit as depressing as these lead-ins. For instance:

  • A Gallup survey reports that 35% of kids in K-12 don’t like reading and 43% never read for fun (Jones, 2022).
  • A National Endowment for the Arts study reports that fewer than half of adults have read a book in the past year (Iyengar, 2024).
  • The National Assessment of Educational Progress finds that only 14% of 8th graders read for enjoyment daily (NAEP, no date).
  • The U.S. Department of Labor says that adults are spending about 25% less time each day reading than they did a decade ago (Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2024).
  • The American Academy of the Arts and Sciences (2023) reports that 84% of adults read for 5 minutes or less on a typical day — only 19% devote such a small amount of time to watching television, playing games, and using computers for personal purposes.
  • The Organisation for Economic Co-operation reveals that the U.S. is near the bottom of 63 countries in how much our 15-year-olds read for pleasure — including many countries whose students cannot read as well as American youths (OECD, 2011).

Independent reports, varied research methodologies, different but large and representative populations … and with consistent conclusions: We don’t read much for enjoyment and we’re reading less than we used to.

The reason? According to a lot of the articles, the problem is our smart phones. The story that they tell is something like: In 2007, Steve Jobs introduced phones that could connect to the internet. Since then, reading in America has waned. Screens displaced books, immediate internet gratification sapped our attention to the point where few can stay on task long enough to read more than 140 characters.

At least those conclusions are often drawn. That’s referred to as displacement theory. We don’t read because screens have displaced reading.

Before conceding the point or exploring solutions (if there are any to be had), let’s contextualize those data and make sure we understand them.

First, I think it’s worth noting that America’s abandonment of reading began long before the smart phone and social media. In the most rigorous and insightful analysis of all this, it’s noted that our reading decline started in 1940s — not the 2000s (Bone, Bu, Sonke, & Francourt, 2025; Canoy, van Ours, & van der Ploeg, 2006; James & Moore, 1940; National Endowment for the Arts, 2007; Robinson, 1980). That’s right, reading had been receding long before these screens were available.

Americans started reading less for pleasure, reading fewer books, and reading less fiction in the 1940s. When FDR was president, we blamed it on movies, radio, and comic books. Later, when I was a kid, television was thought to be the cause, and now it’s due to computer games, the internet, and Tik Tok.

Displacement theory seems accurate when it comes to describing what has taken the place of reading. But that only describes what happened, not why.

It should be acknowledged that this drop in reading has not strictly been an American affair either. Australia and the United Kingdom have experienced similar reading reductions.

None of these reports have indicated how much pleasure reading a society requires for it to be healthy or sound. It appears that observers assume that there is a correct amount of pleasure reading that is needed, and that that amount is what had been common in the recent past.

I’m on board with a society requiring that everyone know how to read. There is clear public good in that. I’m also pleased that this public good can be used by individuals towards their personal happiness (Heath, 1996).

These reports make me wonder, does the freedom to read include a freedom to choose not to?

For the most part, these reports have been mute about what counts as reading. I get that a novel is eligible, but what if I’m interacting on social media?

Also, many of the explanations for the decline in reading point their fingers at the schools. For example, I’ve read that early phonics instruction is turning kids off. That one not coming from the kids but from people who don’t like phonics and who assume children share their contempt.

More recently, I’ve been told that the culprit is the use of short selections to teach reading. That’s provocative, but it neglects that such teaching was universal in the 1940s and 1950s when people read more ((e.g., Dick & Jane, Alice & Jerry), and that a steady decline in pleasure reading accompanied the massive increase book-based reading instruction that took place in the 1990s-2010s (e.g., whole language, Guided Reading, Accelerated Reader, Units of Study).

That reminds me that the many laudatory and considerable efforts taken by teachers to increase kids’ love of reading have neither stemmed nor slowed the turn away from pleasure reading. Think of free reading time (SSR, DEAR), or the proliferation of classroom libraries and book fairs (Scholastic, Reading is Fundamental). The more of those things that we did, the less reading kids chose to do.

All these explanations and attempts at solutions have been well-meaning guesses.

More interesting insights have emerged from scholarly studies. The researchers have been less enamored with the activities that have replaced pleasure reading, and more curious about the conditions that empower or interfere with choice. That work has identified three key variables: reading ability, opportunity to read, and individual purposes.

Ability

Reading for pleasure depends upon readers having sufficient reading ability to engage in the practice. Historically, as more people could read proficiently, the incidence of pleasure reading increased (Heath, 1996).

Reading ability in the U.S. grew steadily from the 1770s to the 1970s (Kaestle, Damen-Moore, Stedman, & Tinsley, 1991). Since then, reading levels have languished — punctuated by brief periods of small improvements or declines. Those ability gains from the 1940s —1970s didn’t prevent a decline in interest in reading, and the most recent pullbacks from reading don’t seem to have been stimulated by any accompanying drops in reading ability.

In fact, one of things that is interesting about the most recently documented declines in reading is that although all the demographics are reading less, the biggest reductions have been experienced by the best readers (Jones, 2022). Perhaps this shift in reading habits by college graduates is a mirror of what has been documented in our universities, that students are not even doing the reading required in their coursework (Baier, 2011) — though this group’s interest in pleasure reading has long been dubious (Jersild, 1931).

There are large numbers of Americans — both adults and children — who do not read very well (NAEP, Kirsch), and consequently, it’s understandable that they may not find reading pleasurable. We should continue to seek ways to expand the literacy franchise in the U.S. However, given the literacy levels already attained and the declines in pleasure reading evident with our best readers, it seems unlikely that higher reading levels are the key to expanded pleasure reading. The gains we are likely to see from such efforts would not be expected to exert an appreciable impact on pleasure reading.

Opportunity

Even if people can read well, they won’t engage in it if there isn’t sufficient opportunity to do so. Opportunity has to do with accessibility, affordability, and time.

It’s much easier to get your hands on a book these days than it was when I was a boy. Bookstore availability grew exponentially from 1940-1980, with the emergence of the sprawling shopping mall chains (e.g., Borders, Daltons, Barnes & Noble), the availability of mass-market paperbacks, and discounts that kept books affordable. Bookstore availability has declined more recently, but that’s been due to the even greater accessibility of books over the internet (e.g., Amazon, Bookshop, Powells). Libraries now offer digital books through services like Libby and Hoopla, meaning that one doesn’t even have to leave home to borrow books.

The children’s book industry has flourished, too — though there are still book deserts in economically-deprived communities (Neuman & Moland, 2019). There are many book charities aimed at addressing that problem and they have managed to distribute tens of millions of books to kids in these neighborhoods (see the charities list on this site).

Leisure time — the time available for pleasure reading — has grown, too, though this shift has been uneven. Adults (25-54) have experienced no improvements in time availability since the 1940s, but young adults and senior citizens both have more leisure time (14-25-year-olds gained 5 hours per week, and the seniors have 14 hours more weekly (Bureau of Labor Statistics, 2024; Krantz-Kent & Stewart, 2007).

There are exceptions to these improvements in opportunity: fewer newspapers are available and the costs of newspapers and magazines have increased more than the rate of inflation. This is also true of comic books. What was a dime comic in 1950, should be $1.40 today given inflation, but comics usually cost four or five dollars. Overall reading is still affordable, but some especially popular choices have gotten pretty pricey!

Overall, opportunity to read in terms of accessibility, affordability and time availability has improved or remained the same for 80 years. The size and universality of the reading declines suggest that they are not likely due to reductions in opportunity to read. Opportunity has not declined; just the opposite. That means people are actively choosing not to read.

Targeted efforts to make reading materials more available in some communities for some audiences could have positive local effects, but increases in opportunity do not seem likely to hold much promise for increasing reading habits.

Goals

Social psychologists have some important insights about the desirability of reading. They find that extroversion — the social, outgoing personality type — is negatively related to reading engagement (Finn, 1997). That means that, all things being equal, some people are just wired to not be turned on to text. Extroverts prefer activities that immerse them in interpersonal connections, an idea personified in popular culture by Marian the librarian (Music Man) or Urkel (Family Matters), socially inept characters lost in their books with few friends.

But personality is complex. Few of us are extroverts or introverts. We are a mix of those — sometimes seeking to be on our own, other times yearning for connection.

There are no data suggesting that more of us are extroverts these days than in the past, though it seems likely that there could be periods when the society goes a bit more one way than the other (think of the COVID tragedy and its aftermath).

The same may be true at certain times of life. The great emphasis on peer relationships during adolescence may be a prime example of that. Social scientists have found a connection between reading and unhappiness with teens, for instance (Csikszentmihalyi & Hunter, 2003). “Teenagers who spent more time during the week [on reading] are generally less happy.” The researchers concluded that reading took time away from interacting with friends and this was the source of the unhappiness. Another possibility not considered by the researchers is that teens with fewer social connections were unhappy, so they read to fill that gap. Either way, this line of research reveals something important about reading that has been ignored in so many of these articles: most readers don’t read to read, they read to fulfill their needs or goals.

Societies change. Some of those changes come about due to technology. That’s why it’s not surprising that some fiction reading may give way to viewing stories in films or on television, or why someone might read more digital texts than printed ones. The same can be said about shifting from newspapers to newsreels in the 1930s, then to the 6:00 news in the 1950s, and now to social media.

But there are other changes, too.

In analyses going back to the 1930s, women/girls have tended to read for pleasure more than men/boys, and their reading has usually included more fiction. Participation by women in the workforce has roughly doubled since 1950 — a shift that would likely alter, not just the amount of their reading, but its focus. These days more women are reading books like Lean In or Machiavelli for Women, leaving them less time for the Outlander novels. Think of all the teacher book clubs and study groups aimed at sharpening professional skills rather than just providing entertainment.

The point is that we read for a purpose; to fulfill needs, to achieve goals, to solve problems, to increase knowledge, to escape, and to make connections. Development — both our personal development and the development of our civilization — may alter the prominence of those purposes from time to time as well as altering the availability of tools to accomplish them.

Reading ability and opportunities to read can impact how much we read. That’s why — if we want to have a society with lots of readers and reading — it matters that we ensure that our schools teach all children to read with great proficiency, that our communities have libraries, and that our tax and mailing policies keep texts of all kinds affordable and accessible.

Nevertheless, lacks of ability and opportunity are not the reason for a reading recession. Nor, frankly, is the increase in the reliance on screens the problem. Screen time may reveal where our reading time is going, but it doesn’t explain the reason for the shift.

Either our purposes have changed — so reading is no longer as pertinent to our lives as it once was — or, we have a proliferation of alternative tools capable of satisfying those needs that reading was addressing.

If we want reading to remain essential, we need to think hard about why we want people to read and how we can best make our children aware of those values. What is it that reading provides that must be preserved? 

In the next blog post, we’ll consider what problems reading can best address and what we can do to let our kids in on those secrets.

The story of a trailblazing scientist whose discoveries about clouds and how they work changed everything we know about weather today. When Joanne Simpson (1923–2010) was a girl, she sailed her boat beneath the puffy white clouds of Cape Cod. As a pilot, she flew her plane so high, its wings almost touched them. And when World War II began and Joanne moved to the University of Chicago, a professor asked her to teach Air Force officers about those very clouds and the weather-changing winds. As soon as the war ended, Joanne decided to seriously study the clouds she had grown to love so much. Her professors laughed. They told her to go home. They told her she was no longer needed. They told her, “No woman ever got a doctorate in meteorology. And no woman ever will.” But Joanne was stubborn. She sold her boat. She flew her last flight. She saved her money so that she could study clouds. She worked so hard and discovered so much that—despite what the professors said—she received a doctorate in meteorology. She was the first woman in the world to do so.

title: Picture Book Power
summary:
Picture Book Power

I’ve always loved that legendary Jeopardy! champion James Holzhauer credited children’s nonfiction picture books for his massive success on the show. It’s a great testament to the fact that picture books are often simply the very best way to make information come alive!

And we need it to come alive, especially when it comes to people who are very nearly forgotten. Sandra Nickel is an award-winning author whose work includes picture book biographies that bring fascinating, often overlooked lives vividly to the page — the creator of nachos Ignacio Anaya in Nacho’s Nachos(opens in a new window), Tiffany lamp designer Clara Driscoll in Making Light Bloom(opens in a new window), astronomer Vera Rubin in The Stuff Between the Stars(opens in a new window), and meteorologist Joanne Simpson in Breaking Through the Clouds(opens in a new window).

Her newest book, The True Ugly Duckling: How Hans Christian Andersen Became a Swan, takes on one of the world’s most beloved storytellers. Sandra tells his story in a way it has never been told before — through a lens that considers what scholars now know of his neurodiversity.

Structured like a fairy tale and illustrated by Calvin Nicholls with extraordinary cut-paper sculptures, this is a book as inventive as its subject and we’re delighted to have Sandra here to share more.

Scissors, Paper, Stories by Sandra Nickel

Hans Christian Andersen said the story of The Ugly Duckling was actually the story of his own life. When I read this, I immediately started looking into why he would say this. What in his life had happened so that he portrayed himself as a duckling who was rejected by everyone he met?

Reading through his autobiographies, it became abundantly clear why he had portrayed himself this way. Andersen had been alone, misunderstood, and bullied before growing up and becoming the famous writer we know as the Father of the Modern Fairytale. I tell of this in The True Ugly Duckling, How Hans Christian Andersen Became a Swan.

Andersen also found a way to comfort himself during his hard times. There are many descriptions about Andersen’s anxiety about life and fitting in. Cutting out shapes, first from cloth and later from paper, soothed him. And when he became immensely popular and was invited by kings and countesses to recite his stories in their castles — something that was nervous-making for Andersen—he continued using this coping technique. 

As he stood in front of the noble guests and told his stories, he took a scissors and paper from his pocket and created a paper cutout at the same time. Since he had been practicing since he was a young child, his cutouts were intricate and beautiful. You can see for yourselves in this “fully cut fairy tale” from the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s website(opens in a new window). 

Because of the importance of paper cutouts to Andersen, Arthur Levine, the editor of The True Ugly Duckling, chose paper sculptor Calvin Nicholls to illustrate Andersen’s life. Nicholls used a different technique from Andersen’s and the result is absolutely stunning.

To connect kids with Hans Christian Andersen and his world of storytelling and paper art, try the activities below.

Biographies as fairytales

Start off by reading the biography, The True Ugly Duckling, How Hans Christian Andersen Became a Swan. It is told in fairytale form, as Andersen told his stories.

Now, ask, “If your life story was told as a fairytale, how would it go?” Would you be a duck, a frog, a nightingale, a swan? Or would you be someone else taken from one of Andersen’s other fairytales? A little mermaid or merman? A prince or princess with a pea? An emperor or empress with “new clothes”?

Then, for an added dimension, have kids cut out shapes from paper as they tell their life stories as fairytales. 

Making paper cutouts

Andersen’s Technique

To try the half-makes-whole paper-cutting technique that is similar to the one Andersen used, gather a scissors and a sheet of paper. Fold the paper in quarters. Along the folded sides, draw half shapes — hearts, diamonds, butterflies, whatever you like. Cut out these half shapes, then unfold your paper and discover the whole you created!

Nicholl’s Technique

To try Calvin Nicholl’s sculpture technique, cut out the shapes that inspire you from different colored paper. For example, if you are paper sculpting a house, cut out walls from one color, windows from another, and the roof from another. (For inspiration, look at Nicholl’s illustration above.) After you’ve finished cutting your shapes, glue them on top of each other. Now, sit back and admire the paper sculpture you’ve created.

Wishing you all a wonderful time with fairy tales and paper cutouts!

title: AI and Reading Comprehension Instruction: Part 2
summary:
AI and Reading Comprehension Instruction: Part 2

The world’s all atingle with artificial intelligence (AI).

OpenAI reports that ChatGPT serves 700 million users each week. Seventy-eight percent of businesses and other organizations depend upon it, too. Private investment in AI is more than $100 billion in the U.S. alone.

Given that, it shouldn’t be surprising that the nose of this technology camel is poking under the Education tent. Even when educators eschew it, students themselves find ways to bring it in.  

In my last blog entry, I decried some uses of AI in the teaching of reading comprehension. My concern was that these would do more to undermine kids’ progress than to facilitate it.

Much of my criticism was based on a fundamental truism: Nobody can learn for you. We all must do our own learning.

When students read a text and summarize it, they may or may not learn something. But when AI does this summarizing, a lack of learning is guaranteed.

Think of some analogous non-tech examples:

Mom finds out about Janey’s homework assignment at bedtime. She insists her little darling sleep, but has an older sibling complete the work so Janey won’t get in trouble. I don’t know if the big sister will learn something, but it’s certain it will be a zero for Janey.

Butch, the hulking football star, bullies a nerdy classmate into completing his book report. You don’t need an fMRI scan of their brains to recognize that in the game of learning, Butch fumbled.

Even when students seemingly do the work, AI may manage to prevent learning.

Reading comprehension instruction tends to focus too much on how to answer certain kinds of questions and not enough on how to understand text. Question types don’t explain variance in reading achievement, but differences in text complexity do (ACT, 2006). If kids can make sense of text, they can answer any type of question.

Comprehension instruction should focus on world knowledge, complexity and extensiveness of content, vocabulary, syntax, cohesion, discourse structure, literary devices, data presentation devices, tone, bias, genre differences, and so on. Readers need to know how to negotiate these text features (Shanahan, 2025).

That’s why the use of AI to revise texts to facilitate comprehension is such a bad idea. The ability of AI to reliably transform a fifth-grade text into a third grade one without losing or damaging content has not yet been proven. But even when it manages to accomplish that, it strips away or transforms those text features students should be learning to deal with.

Altering the readability of a text — when done well — may ease reading comprehension. But such alterations reduce the possibility that the reading will contribute to improved comprehension.

That might make me sound like a technophobe, striving to keep those nasty modern technologies out of our schools; a charter member of the Luddites Are Us Club.

Nothing of the kind.

Students must do certain things if they are to become good comprehenders. They need to read lots of texts and use information gained from that reading: discussing it with others, writing about it, applying it to problems. The texts they read for this purpose need to be challenging — not much is gained from focusing on texts that can already be read reasonably well. Teaching should help students learn how to surmount text features that may block understanding, and as they gain purchase of those barriers, they become better readers.

That, I believe, is a good place for artificial intelligence to come in. Instead of helping kids to evade and avoid those challenges, it should help teachers to guide kids to deal with them.

When I speak to teachers about teaching reading with complex text, I offer examples of some of those barriers and the kinds of teaching that would help students to solve the texts.

Almost always, I’m asked by teachers (some displaying considerable embarrassment), how can I know which sentences (or cohesive links) might trip up students’ comprehension? I usually give an answer like: “Look for especially long sentences, sentences with a lot of internal punctuation, sentences with multiple clauses or phrases, sentences in passive voice, and so on.” They often nod skeptically, revealing uncertainty, a lack of confidence.

I’ve decided that a better answer is to use artificial intelligence. Teachers don’t have the time to do a thorough analysis of these kinds of text features, and AI can do a reasonably good job of identifying them. With that assistance, teachers can choose which ones they want to address, considering their students and their time constraints.

For instance, I entered into ChatGPT the text for the story How the Camel Got His Hump by Rudyard Kipling, and asked, “What are the five most complex sentences — sentences that might confuse young readers?”

It spit out five sentences, along with explanations as to why they were chosen. Here are three of them:

“In the beginning of years, when the world was so new and all, and the Animals were just beginning to work for Man, there was a Camel, and he lived in the middle of a Howling Desert because he did not want to work; and besides, he was a Howler himself.”

“So he ate sticks and thorns and tamarisks and milkweed and prickles, most ‘scruciating idle; and when anybody spoke to him he said ‘Humph!’ Just ‘Humph!’ and no more.”

“At the end of the day the Man called the Horse and the Dog and the Ox together, and said, ‘Three, O Three, I’m very sorry for you (with the world so new-and-all); but that Humph-thing in the Desert can’t work, or he would have been here by now, so I am going to leave him alone, and you must work double-time to make up for it.’”

All five would be potentially useful for syntax teaching, and Kipling tales are particularly good selections for a heavy emphasis on syntax. In this case, I wanted to emphasize the third sentence. ChatGPT’s explanation for the choice is that it includes dialogue embedded in a long sentence, several clauses joined by commas and semi-colons, and the figurative phrase, “Humph-thing.”

I’d ask the kids, “Why was the Man angry at the Humph-thing?” or “Why did the Man apologize to the Horse, Dog and Ox?” or “Why might the Horse, Dog, and Ox dislike the Camel?” Those questions can be answered with information from that sentence. If they can answer, then the sentence was not a barrier to comprehension. If they could not, then I’d teach them how to make sense of it, focusing on the quotation marks, figuring out how to break it into parts, and so on.

I wasn’t surprised that AI could identify complex sentences and uncover what made them complicated and potentially confusing. I didn’t ask it to suggest comprehension questions for those sentences. Experience tells me it can do that well.

What about potential barriers that may be harder to determine, like cohesive links? These are important because they connect the ideas in a text.

I entered an episode of Antoine de Saint-Exupéry’s The Little Prince and asked, “Can you show me some of the cohesive ties in this text?” It provided several so I followed up with, “Do any of these appear to be especially difficult for readers to recognize?”

It nominated several possibilities. For instance, consider this complex linkage of ideas:

“I cannot play with you,” the fox said. “I am not tamed.”

“Ah! Please excuse me,” said the little prince.

But, after some thought, he added:

“What does that mean — ‘tame’?”… [8 intervening sentences] …

“It is an act too often neglected,” said the fox. “It means to establish ties.”… [48 intervening sentences]…

If you want a friend, tame me…”

To make sense of this exchange, readers must connect tame, establish ties, and friendship, something hard to do given the distance between their mentions in the text.

My AI helper also pointed out some reappearance of concepts in this text without exact repetition: unique-important, men-hunters, and ellipsis (omissions of words the reader must fill in): “‘On another planet?’ ‘Yes.’” (A full sentence response would be: “Yes, it is on another planet.”)

Those were helpful, but I was especially pleased with the identification of parallel structure or pattern repetition in this text. In this short episode, the terms “to me” and “to you” are repeated 9 times. ChatGPT pointed out that this reinforced text cohesion throughout through rhythm and structure.

For me, this structure emphasizes that this conversation is a meeting of the minds of two strangers who come together from very different perspectives. They are trying to communicate and connect, but they also want to maintain their view and to make certain the other recognizes this. By reiterating that what is being stated is my opinion or my point of view (“to me”) makes this clear. This is a wonderful example of the structure of the text conveying or reinforcing the information that is being stated in the words themselves. Kids need to learn that authors repeat themselves for a reason and it is worth noting those repetitions and thinking about the reason for them.

I made some other requests of AI, too, asking it to identify multiple themes or tone (and what words or structures the author used to convey tone). Tone refers to the atmosphere of a text and reveals an author’s attitude towards the subject at hand or the characters. A text may be funny, sad, playful, nostalgic, frightening, authoritative, and so on.

In all these cases, AI provided more than I could possibly teach in one set of lessons. I liked having the options, and, of course, by querying AI more specifically, I may end up with fewer choices but ones particularly relevant to my curricular goals. Even with that, a teacher will need to make the choices. Perhaps the items that AI identifies will be too easy for your students or irrelevant to your goals.

As you can see from these examples, artificial intelligence can be a useful tool for helping develop more powerful comprehension lessons. Instead of using it to remove barriers to comprehension, use it to identify the barriers and then show students how to surmount them.

When it comes to reading comprehension, our job isn’t to smooth their way, to avoid and evade difficulty. No, we are responsible for making students powerful and independent, teaching them how to recognize and transcend linguistic and conceptual obstacles. 

AI has a role to play in the teaching of reading comprehension. But that role should involve it as an assistant to the teacher, not to the reader.

A large study of more than 3,700 dream and waking reports found that what we experience during sleep is shaped by both our personalities and the world around us. Rather than simply replaying daily events, the dreaming brain mixes memories, emotions, imagined possibilities, and familiar settings into vivid new scenarios.

title: Scientists discover how the brain rewires itself to truly multitask
summary: Practice may do more than make perfect. Researchers found that extensive training physically reorganizes the brain, allowing learned tasks to bypass the prefrontal cortex and run through specialized circuits instead. By freeing the brain's "thinking" center, people became better at performing another task at the same time, challenging the long-held idea that humans only switch rapidly between tasks rather than truly multitask.

title: Common constipation drug may help clear depression brain fog
summary: An existing constipation drug may have an unexpected new use: helping clear the "brain fog" that often lingers after depression. In a small clinical trial, people with a history of depression who took the medication prucalopride for about a week performed better on tests of memory, attention, and thinking speed than those who received a placebo. The drug targets a serotonin receptor found in both the gut and the brain, and researchers saw no significant side effects.

title: Alzheimer's tau protein has a surprising secret role in memory
summary: Researchers found that tau is essential for turning new experiences into lasting memories by helping organize the brain's memory-storing cells. The mouse study also revealed how abnormal tau may contribute to Alzheimer's by disrupting both the formation of new memories and the recall of existing ones.

title: They knew the pill was fake but their memory still improved
summary: Healthy older adults experienced measurable improvements in memory, physical performance, and stress after taking placebo pills for just three weeks. The most surprising finding was that the placebo often worked even when participants knew the pills were completely inactive.

title: Scientists stunned as bumble bees solve a classic intelligence test
summary: Bumble bees astonished researchers by inventing a new way to reach a hidden reward, despite never being taught the trick. The discovery adds to growing evidence that these tiny insects are far smarter and more adaptable than once believed.

title: Scientists found an early depression clue hidden in children’s eyes
summary: Depression appears to change what children notice in the faces around them, but the effect depends on family history. Kids with a higher inherited risk became more focused on sadness, while lower-risk children lost some of their natural attention to happy expressions.

title: Why middle age is becoming a breaking point in the U.S.
summary: A new international study finds that middle-aged Americans are lonelier, more depressed, and experiencing worse memory and health than earlier generations. Researchers say growing financial strain, weaker social supports, and chronic stress may explain why the U.S. is falling behind other wealthy nations.

title: Learning a musical instrument in your 70s could help protect memory
summary: Learning a musical instrument later in life may help keep the brain younger for longer. In a four-year study, older adults who continued practicing maintained their memory performance and showed less age-related brain shrinkage than those who quit. The benefits were especially noticeable in brain regions tied to memory and learning.

title: Why grandparents matter more than ever for children's mental health
summary: A child psychologist says grandparents are more important than ever as youth mental health challenges continue to rise. He argues that children need supportive relationships, meaningful conversations, and a sense of purpose—not just pressure to achieve. Grandparents can help by listening, encouraging, and creating positive experiences that strengthen emotional resilience.

title: Caffeine reversed memory problems caused by sleep deprivation
summary: Scientists discovered that sleep deprivation damages a key brain circuit responsible for social memory, making it harder to recognize familiar individuals. In laboratory studies, caffeine restored communication between neurons in this pathway and reversed the memory deficits caused by lost sleep. The effect was remarkably targeted, helping the impaired circuit recover without overstimulating normal brain function.

title: A 100-year-old piano mystery has finally been solved
summary: For more than a century, pianists and music teachers have argued over whether a performer’s touch can actually change the tone color of a piano note — and now scientists say the answer is yes. Using a cutting-edge sensor system that tracked piano key movements at 1,000 frames per second, researchers discovered that elite pianists subtly manipulate keys in ways that listeners can genuinely hear, even if they’ve never played piano before.

title: Mindfulness may lower blood pressure in just 8 weeks
summary: Mindfulness, gratitude, and optimism training may improve blood pressure, inflammation, and other heart-health measures within just eight to 12 weeks. The strongest programs paired daily practice with regular reinforcement, suggesting that improving psychological well-being could become another tool for protecting cardiovascular health.

title: Scientists find a human-only gene that may help explain our brainpower
summary: Scientists discovered that human microglia, immune cells that help shape developing brain circuits, can take four to eight years to mature instead of just weeks as they do in mice. The unusually slow process may help explain how the human brain develops its remarkable complexity and cognitive abilities.

title: HEPA air purifiers may boost brain function after just one month
summary: Adults aged 40 and older performed about 12% faster on a test of executive function after using a HEPA air purifier at home for one month. The findings suggest that cleaner indoor air could offer a simple way to help protect the brain from the effects of traffic-related pollution.

title: Scientists challenge a 70-year-old “lizard brain” myth
summary: A long-standing picture of brain evolution as newer, rational layers stacked on top of an ancient “lizard brain” may be deeply misleading. Researchers found that evolution instead appears to balance two competing styles of brain wiring, expanding one while shrinking the other depending on what an animal needs to survive.

title: Reaching 90 without dementia doesn’t mean you’re in the clear
summary: A study of people over 90 found that dementia risk remains strongly shaped by sex, race and genetics, with women and black participants facing notably higher risks. Intriguingly, some people stayed cognitively healthy despite carrying major risk factors, potentially offering clues to how the brain can resist dementia deep into old age.

title: Your sleep may be hiding an early clue to Alzheimer’s
summary: Frequent micro-awakenings during sleep were linked to higher genetic risk for Alzheimer’s in healthy middle-aged adults who had no symptoms. The discovery raises the possibility that subtle changes during sleep could offer an early warning signal years before memory problems appear.

title: Researchers followed 400,000 kids for 20 years and found a lasting pre-K advantage
summary: A 20-year study of 400,000 students found that children who attended public school pre-K earned better grades and test scores through high school than those in other childcare settings. Better-trained teachers and earlier exposure to structured classrooms may help explain why the advantage lasted so long.

title: Smart nanoparticles light up brain cancer and destroy what surgery misses
summary: Scientists created smart nanoparticles that can both illuminate hidden glioblastoma cells during surgery and destroy microscopic cancer left behind afterward. In mice, the treatment prevented recurrence and led to 100% survival at 60 days, though it has not yet been tested in humans.

title: Scientists discover a brain “brake” that can shut down chronic pain
summary: Researchers discovered a brain-based “brake” that can shut down chronic nerve pain in mice by calming an overactive pain circuit. Targeting this system more precisely could one day lead to powerful pain relief without affecting opioid receptors throughout the entire body.

title: Too much or too little sleep may make your body age faster
summary: Both too little and too much sleep may be linked to faster aging throughout the body. Researchers analyzing 23 biological aging clocks found the lowest aging levels among people sleeping about 6.4 to 7.8 hours per day. Short or long sleep was also associated with numerous conditions affecting the brain, heart, lungs, metabolism, and digestive system.

title: Childhood trauma may leave a lasting “scar” inside brain cells
summary: Early-life stress may physically alter how DNA is packaged in the brain, leaving stress-related genes primed to activate more easily years later. In mice, researchers were able to block this effect, preventing the heightened anxiety and stress sensitivity that otherwise appeared in adulthood.

title: Your brain may not actually “make” decisions
summary: A neuroscientist is challenging the idea that the brain contains a central system that actually “makes” our decisions. What we experience as choosing may instead emerge from the continuous interaction of perception, movement, the body, and the world around us.

title: Depression may shut down the brain’s ability to make new neurons
summary: A major study found that adults with depression show disrupted production of new neurons in the hippocampus, potentially weakening the brain’s ability to separate new experiences from painful memories. The researchers also identified broad molecular changes that could open the door to new treatments tailored to different biological forms of depression.

title: Shingles vaccine linked to 24% lower dementia risk
summary: Older adults who received the Shingrix shingles vaccine were 24% less likely to be diagnosed with dementia over four years in a study of more than 500,000 people. Researchers estimate the difference could amount to roughly one dementia case prevented for every 17 people vaccinated.

title: Quitting alcohol may prime the brain for relapse
summary: Mice that developed compulsive drinking after alcohol abstinence showed more than double the activity in a brain region associated with stress and addiction. Because the signal appeared before they drank again, researchers think it could eventually help predict who is most at risk of relapse.

title: This common vitamin was linked to 13% better cognitive scores
summary: Older adults with mild cognitive impairment and sleep problems who took at least 5,000 IU of vitamin D daily scored more than 13% higher on a cognitive test than those taking none. The preliminary findings suggest vitamin D could be worth studying as a potentially modifiable factor during an early window of cognitive decline.

title: A major Alzheimer’s risk gene may shrink brain cells years before symptoms
summary: Researchers have uncovered a possible reason why the Alzheimer’s risk gene APOE4 can disrupt the brain long before memory problems begin. In mice, APOE4 increased a protein called Nell2, shrinking neurons and making memory circuits unusually active. That early hyperactivity predicted worse memory later in life. Reducing Nell2 in adult mice reversed the abnormal changes, raising hopes for a new way to intervene before Alzheimer’s progresses.

title: Multilingual people may have brains up to 13 years younger
summary: People who speak several languages may have brains that age more slowly, with four-language speakers showing brains that appeared about 13 years younger than those of monolinguals. Starting earlier and becoming highly fluent were also linked to a stronger effect.

title: Schizophrenia’s lost brain connections follow a surprising pattern
summary: Specialized brain scans reveal that schizophrenia is linked to widespread loss of the synapses that connect brain cells, with the left side of the brain hit especially hard. The damage follows a surprisingly organized pattern tied to the brain’s chemistry and wiring. Researchers also identified a left frontal region that may serve as a starting point for the loss.

title: Ozempic does something unexpected to the brain’s hunger neurons
summary: Ozempic may work in the brain in almost the opposite way scientists expected, activating hunger-linked neurons that appear essential for sustaining fat loss. The surprising discovery in mice could reveal new targets for developing even more effective obesity drugs.
